title: SRE documentation: SLOs, error budgets, capacity planning, reliability initiatives, incident review standards, and runbooks
author: Ari Chen
content:
Summary

This document defines Redwood Inference's SRE documentation standards covering SLOs and error budgets, capacity planning, reliability initiatives, incident review standards, operational tooling, and runbook requirements. It provides templates, measurable thresholds, ownership, and required cadence for review. The goal is to ensure consistent service-level objectives, predictable capacity behavior, and repeatable post-incident learning across inference services (hosted API, Dedicated, and Private).

1) Principles and scope

- Audience: SREs, service owners, platform engineers, and product managers.
- Scope: All production-facing inference services and control-plane components that directly impact customer-facing latency, throughput, or correctness. This includes: model-serving API, routing layer, cache service, KV cache store, batching service, and observability pipeline.
- Principles: measurable SLOs, time-bounded error budgets, proactive capacity planning, blameless postmortems, automated operational tooling, and living runbooks.

2) SLOs and error budgets (policy)

Overview
- Every production service must declare at least one availability or correctness SLO and one latency SLO where applicable.
- SLOs must be customer-centric (e.g., successful responses, 95th/99th percentile latency for tail-sensitive services).

SLO structure (required fields for each SLO)
- SLO name: short descriptive name (e.g., model-serving-api-success-rate).
- SLO type: availability | latency | correctness | throughput.
- Objective: numeric target with percentile and window (e.g., 99.95% successful responses per 30d).
- Measurement method: data source and query (e.g., datadog metric "api.request.success_ratio" aggregated over rolling 30d).
- Owner: service owner and SRE on-call.
- Error budget policy: burn thresholds and automated actions (see below).

Required SLOs (examples)
- model-serving-api-success-rate: availability, objective = 99.95% successful requests (30d window), measured from edge gateway success ratio.
- model-serving-latency-p95: latency, objective = p95 <= 150ms (7d window) for non-streaming text-generation endpoints.
- embedding-service-p99: latency, objective = p99 <= 400ms (30d window).
- control-plane-availability: availability, objective = 99.9% (30d window).

Error budget policy (standard)
- Error budget = 100% - SLO objective (over the defined window).
- Burn thresholds and actions:
  - Green (<= 25% budget spent): normal operations.
  - Yellow (25% - 75% budget spent): SRE and service owner to review weekly; consider mitigations.
  - Red (> 75% budget spent): mandatory incident review and temporary mitigation plan; restrict risky rollouts and model changes.
  - Crisis (> 100% budget spent): immediate incident response and executive notification.

Automated enforcement
- Integrations: Datadog monitors calculate rolling SLO burn rate; PagerDuty escalation on Red/Crisis thresholds.
- Runbooks must include exact queries and dashboard links for each SLO.

3) Capacity planning (process and model)

Signals and inputs
- Historical QPS and token/sec trends (90/95/99 quantiles).
- Model memory and compute profiles (peak sequence length distributions, KV cache hit rates).
- Autoscaling behavior and observed cooldowns.
- Business signals: expected customer growth, marketing campaigns, new product launches.

Capacity model (required items)
- Per-service capacity unit: define a normalized unit (e.g., tokens-per-second per GPU type).
- Headroom policy: maintain 40% steady-state headroom for hosted API at regional level; Dedicated contracts follow SLA-linked reserve.
- Burst capacity: support up to 2x normal peak for up to 15 minutes for safety-critical endpoints.
- Failure domain planning: capacity must be provisioned across at least two AZs/regions for critical services.

Cadence and deliverables
- Quarterly capacity review: forecasting through 12 months with monthly slices. Responsible: SRE capacity lead + product.
- Pre-launch checklist for new features/models: 30/14/3/1 day readiness checkpoints (load-tests, canaries, metric baselines).
- Scaling runbooks: documented steps for manual scale-up in the event of autoscaler failure.

Capacity runbook (summary steps)
1. Confirm observed QPS and token/sec in the last 60m and 24h.
2. Check autoscaler logs and scaling history dashboard.
3. If autoscaler failed or lagging: follow manual scale procedure (CLI commands, terraform run, or orchestration UI steps included below).
4. Rebalance traffic using smart-routing to reduce pressure on saturated pools.
5. Open incident and notify stakeholders; schedule follow-up capacity review.

4) Reliability initiatives (programs and prioritization)

Program types
- Infrastructure hardening: kernel GPU drivers, network egress controls, and node replacement processes.
- Observability improvements: sampling upgrades, end-to-end distributed tracing for request lifecycles, and synthetic traffic for accuracy and latency.
- Cost vs reliability experiments: targeted canary quantization or batching adjustments for cost reduction with SLO guardrails.

Prioritization framework
- Impact (customer exposure, revenue, or compliance) x Effort (engineering weeks) score.
- At least one cross-team initiative per quarter with SRE sponsorship.

Example initiatives (current)
- Improved KV cache eviction policy to reduce cold-start token cost (owner: serving-runtime).
- Regional failover automation to reduce mean time to recover (MTTR) by 40% (owner: eng-platform + SRE).

5) Incident review and postmortem standards

Goals
- Produce blameless, action-oriented postmortems for P1/P2 incidents and any SLO breaches causing Red/Crisis error-budget states.

Required timeline
- Initial incident summary posted within 24 hours.
- Draft postmortem within 72 hours.
- Final postmortem published and action items assigned within 7 days.

Postmortem template (required sections)
- Title and incident ID
- Summary (one-paragraph customer impact summary)
- Severity and duration (timeline of major events)
- Impacted services and customers
- Root cause analysis (technical findings)
- Contributing factors (people, process, tooling)
- Actions taken during incident
- Action items (owner, due date, verification criteria)
- Lessons learned and follow-up plan
- Link to runbooks, dashboards, and recordings

Action item policy
- Every postmortem must list at least one permanent corrective action unless the incident was caused by an external third-party outage; temporary mitigations must have expiration and follow-up actions.
- Owners must verify remediation completion and provide verification data (metrics or tests) within the assigned due date.

6) Operational tooling (dashboards, alerts, and automation)

Standard dashboards (required)
- SLO overview dashboard: rolling burn rate, per-SLO time series, top error reasons.
- Service health dashboard: latency percentiles, success ratio, token throughput, queue depths, GPU utilization by pool.
- Capacity dashboard: current capacity units, headroom percentage, autoscaler health, and pending scale events.

Alerting policy
- Alert on symptoms (high error rate, request queue growth) and on infrastructure signals (node OOM, GPU driver restarts).
- Alert thresholds must be tied to SLOs and configured to minimize noisy alerts: include a required 3-step tuning before promotion to on-call.
- All alerts must include runbook link and suggested initial remediation steps.

Automation and runbook integration
- Where possible, automate mitigations that are low-risk and repeatable (traffic rebalancing, autoscaler restart, cache warm-up).
- Playbooks must expose a single-click or CLI step for common recoveries and safe rollback operations for model rollouts.

Tooling inventory (minimum required)
- Metrics: Datadog (metrics/SLO calculation).
- Tracing: Honeycomb or Jaeger for request flows.
- Logging: ELK/Cloud logging with retention policy per service.
- Alerting: PagerDuty.
- Incident tracking: Jira + Confluence for postmortems.
- Capacity planning: internal capacity workbook (spreadsheet) linked from dashboard.

7) SRE runbooks (templates and example)

Runbook requirements
- Every runbook must be short, actionable, and include: detection steps, verification queries, step-by-step remediation, rollback steps, impact and risk, and owners.
- Include exact CLI commands, terraform module names, orchestration UI links, and required IAM roles.
- Keep runbooks under 1-2 pages; use links for detailed procedures.

Runbook template (short)
- Name
- Service and team
- Detection (metrics/alerts that trigger runbook)
- Immediate mitigation (1-3 steps)
- Deep mitigation (if immediate mitigation fails)
- Rollback criteria and steps
- Verification and closure criteria
- Post-incident actions

Example runbook: model-serving-api-high-queue
- Detect: alert when request_queue_depth > 1000 for 5m OR p95 latency > 300ms for 3m.
- Immediate mitigation:
  1) Reduce ingress: enable rate-limit gate for non-critical keys via routing console (link: /ops/routing).
  2) Rebalance: move 20% traffic from saturated pool to secondary pool using smart-routing (CLI: redwoodctl routing shift --from pool-a --to pool-b --percent 20).
  3) Restart autoscaler process on control-plane node (systemctl restart redwood-autoscaler).
- Deep mitigation:
  1) Manually scale GPU pool (terraform apply -var 'pool_size=20' modules/gpu_pool).
  2) Temporarily disable non-essential background workloads (batch jobs).
- Rollback: reverse routing changes and restore normal rate limits once queue depth < 200 and p95 latency < 120ms for 10 minutes.
- Verification: check SLO dashboard and Datadog queries; confirm queue depth and latency metrics stable for 30 minutes.

8) Ownership, review cadence, and documentation hygiene

- Owners: Each service SLO must list a primary owner (service PM or engineering lead) and an SRE owner.
- Quarterly reviews: SLOs, error budget policies, and runbooks reviewed at least quarterly by service owner and SRE.
- Documentation hygiene: update date required in runbook header; orphaned runbooks without updates for > 180 days are flagged for review.

9) Appendix: example SLO table and measurement queries

- Example SLO table (CSV style):
  name, type, objective, window, measurement_source, owner
  model-serving-api-success-rate, availability, 99.95%, 30d, datadog:api.request.success_ratio, @service-owner
  model-serving-latency-p95, latency, p95<=150ms, 7d, datadog:api.request.latency.p95, @sre-oncall

- Example Datadog query (availability):
  numerator: sum:requests.success{service:model-serving-api}.rollup(sum, 60)
  denominator: sum:requests.total{service:model-serving-api}.rollup(sum, 60)
  success_ratio = numerator / denominator

- Example Datadog query (p95 latency):
  p95:percentile(95):trace.duration{service:model-serving-api}.rollup(max, 60)

10) How to get help and next steps

- For immediate SRE on-call help: PagerDuty -> SRE escalation policy.
- For documentation changes: open a consolidated PR in the SRE documentation Git repo and ping #sre-docs on Slack.
- Next review: scheduled for 2027-02-01.
